name: Nopala Chatino
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Glottolog cites only McIntosh 2011 subclassification comments; no grammar/phonology of the Nopala variety located; Chatino overviews consulted carry no stress statement.

new_statements.quote: Se usa aquí el alfabeto elaborado en el análisis preliminar del chatino de Nopala. [...] 1. Las palabras chatinas se pronuncian con mayor fuerza en la última sílaba y no llevan acento escrito. Por ejemplo: jija 'tortilla', jica 'palo'.
new_statements.translation: The alphabet used here is the one developed in the preliminary analysis of Nopala Chatino. [...] 1. Chatino words are pronounced with greater force on the last syllable and carry no written accent. For example: jija 'tortilla', jica 'stick'.
new_statements.citation: Wardle, Edward & Linda Wardle. 1980. Cuento 'ine' cha'tño: narraciones en chatino de Nopala, Oaxaca. Tlalocan 8: 251-256. doi:10.19130/iifl.tlalocan.1980.52 (UNAM, open access).
new_statements.locator: p. 256, 'Aclaraciones sobre el Alfabeto', item 1 (PDF page 6 of 6)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the final syllable of the word (the examples jija, jica show that Nopala retains disyllabic words, so 'last syllable' is not vacuous). Corroborated for the Teotepec variety of the same ISO/Glottolog language by McIntosh 2015 p. 44: 'Syllable stress in Chatino occurs on the ultimate syllable (Upson and Longacre, 1965; Pride, 1997). In monosyllabic varieties of Chatino stress occurs on the syllable.' (repeated p. 217, sec. 6.2.1) — Teotepec words are monosyllabic, so stress sits on the sole (= final) syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Wardle & Wardle 1980: none. McIntosh 2015 p. 217 lists lexemes that violate the one-syllable phonological word (Spanish names /liF pa/ 'Felipa', /RiF ke/ 'Enrique', some compounds, 'a handful of rogue disyllables e.g. jakwa four') but does not say where stress falls in them.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('las palabras chatinas'), stated as an orthographic note justifying the absence of a written accent; based on the authors' 'preliminary analysis' (their 1975 SIL 'Phonemics Statement', not obtained). McIntosh's statement is about the syllable/phonological word (= stem) and is itself a generalisation citing Upson & Longacre 1965 (comparative Chatino) and Pride 1997 (Panixtlahuaca), not a Teotepec-specific finding; the language is tonal (McIntosh: nine tones, fourteen tone sequences), and neither source discusses phonetic correlates of stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Two first-hand statements, both inside Glottolog's nopa1235/cya (which has no dialect children): (1) Wardle & Wardle 1980 describe the Chatino of Santos Reyes Nopala itself (district of Juquila; consultants Antonio Quintas, Leoncio Quintas, Melchor Zarate) — the namesake variety; (2) McIntosh 2015 describes Santa Lucia Teotepec Eastern Chatino (agencia of the municipio Santos Reyes Nopala), which he labels ISO 639-3 cya and which Glottolog Caution: Glottolog's third 'med' and WALS's sole source for cht, McKaughan 1954 'Chatino formulas and phonemes', is a description of Yaitepec Eastern Chatino (a separate Glottolog language) per Sullivant 2015 p. 34; only McKaughan & McKaughan 1951 (vocabulary) is Nopala.

sources.note: p. 256 alphabet note: Chatino words are pronounced with greater force on the last syllable, hence no written accent (examples jija 'tortilla', jica 'palo'). Nopala proper.

sources.note: p. 44 (sec. 2.3.1): 'Syllable stress in Chatino occurs on the ultimate syllable (Upson and Longacre, 1965; Pride, 1997). In monosyllabic varieties of Chatino stress occurs on the syllable.' p. 217 (sec. 6.2.1): 'Regarding prosodic features, syllable stress in monosyllabic varieties of Chatino occurs on the syllable.' Teotepec (ISO cya); phonological word = one syllable; disyllabic loans/compounds noted without a stress rule.

sources.note: Family-level only: Table 5 Zapotecan 24 languages = 8 monosyllabic-root, 3 root-initial, 8 root-final, 3 root-penultimate, 2 variable; Chatino languages not itemized; 'stress is... always confined to roots/stems'.

sources.note: Used only for its bibliography of Nopala sources (p. 34): McKaughan & McKaughan 1951 = 'a vocabulary of Nopala Eastern Chatino'; McKaughan 1954 = Yaitepec phonemes; Nopala retains vowel length (p. 133). Its own stress statement (stem-final, p. 54) concerns Tataltepec, a different language.

sources.citation: Campbell, Eric. 2013. The internal diversification and subgrouping of Chatino. IJAL 79(3): 395-420.
sources.note: Family-level: Eastern Chatino words reduced to one syllable 'via the loss of non-prominent vowels, where prominent vowels are those in root-final syllables' (p. 401); Zapotec root-initial prominence is 'the opposite of Chatino' (fn. 10).
